The curious and important operation of transfusion of blood was recently performed with perfect success by Mr John Wilson and Mr. Richard Ripley, of Whitby, on the person of .Mrs. Hartley, who was rapidly Sinking under violent hemorrhage. The pulse was gone, and not even by the application of a mirror to the mouth of the patient could it be perceived that she breathed; hut, by the injection into her veins of a large quantity of blood, taken from those of her sister and husband, the patient was gradually withdrawn from the very jaws of death, and is now approaching convalescence. þÿ Sunderland I let aid.

The Scold's Bridle revived. þÿ At the mayor's office, Stafford, last week, Mary, wife of Thomas Careless, of the Broad Eye, a perfect termagant, was ordered to pay Is. penalty, and 7s (id. costs, for an unprovoked assault on Mary, the wife of Lewis Bromley During the investigation her garrulity was so incessant, that the mayor was under the necessity of sending for the " scold's bridle," an iron instrument, of very antique construction, which in olden times was occasionally called into use. It is formed of an elliptical bow of iron, enclosing the head from the lower extremity of one ear to the other, with a transverse piece of iron extending from the nape of the neck to the mouth, from which projects a flat bit, which enters the mouth, and completely covers the tongue, preventing its movement, and the whole machinery, when adjusted, is locked at the back of the head. The bridle is to be put in thorough repair, and hung in terorem in the mayor's office, and used as occasion may call it forth. þÿ London paper.

From the New York Albion, July 7, 1838. THE PHYSICAL EDUCATION OF CHILDREN. BV RICHARD BURKE, M. D.

There can be little doubt that much of the misery of after-life springs from the mismanagement of the infant state. It is not alone sufficient that those who have the bringing up of children should guard against noxious and malignant disease, which with very little care may easily be effected. A more imperitive and arduous duty is that which calls upon us to prepare, by a proper and suitable course of daily exercise, a healthy habit of body which will necessarily impart to mind, in all its trying and harassing speculations, its powerful influence. When the frame and muscular system are fully developed, there is a marked equanimity of life, unknown to those whose persons are weakly and infirm. In the management of infant life, the first thing which demands our attention is the supply of food. Every one knows the old saving of a þÿchild sstomach being like a schoolboy, doing mischief, if not employed in digestion. This I consider as one of the greatest errors that ever escaped from a great man; but Rush could give currency, in his day, to the most absurd paradox. There are organs of our frame which require a period of repose quite as much as the muscles of voluntary motion ; of these, the stomach is one. It is admitted that a þÿchild stomach s is more active than that of a full grown person, and that it more readily disposes of its contents, Few things demand from us greater attention than the supply of food. The common practice of cramming the stomach of a child because it is growing, is a coarse view

of animal growth. It thus becomes overloaded, and altogether suspends digestion. In very early life the child is unable to take that exercise which at a later period maintains a proper distribution of its growing powers. þÿ þÿ or At this age some of the organs have not yet assumed that healthy developernent which they afterwards attain. Of these the liver is one, whose bile is not of that healthy quality which at a more advanced period of life it is found. It is insipid, and more or less of a gelatinous nature, carrying with it, too often, acrid matter, which no other organ can neutralise. New fluids are thus generated, which at this particular age produce injurious eflects upon some delicate organ. The brain is perhaps the organ which suffers most at this age. It has not yet lost its preternatural size, but attracts an increased quantity of blood. Not having attained the degree of firmness and density which it subsequently attains, it is less able to resist the impetus of blood to j which it yields, terminating frequently in ef- | fusion into the ventricles, known by the common name of water on the brain. As chil- | dren grow up, this predisposition is overcome, provided positive disease be not already established ; for the demand which is now made for blood, by every other organ and muscle of the body, equalises its distribution. The dress of children is a subject of deep interest. I cannot too strongly condemn the practice, which still prevails in manv families of enveloping young children in endless folds
of clothing, which, in almost every instance, checks and controls the proper developernent of their little mruscles, leaving upon thousands lasting traces of its bad ellccts.

3D&1T33S TiaafrasroisKR mamra&asma A child, even at its earliest moments, requires an unrestrained freedom for its little limbs. To this nature prompts, as the only means of developing its muscular system, which we ought to favour by encumbering them as little as possible with clothing. The freedom of action which those little creatures thus enjoy, distributes to every organ and muscle its fair share of the animating principle of fluid of life. The efforts which young children, when cased in this mummy manner make, soon exhausts their strength, arid a waste of animal matter is effected without adding to the general developernent of the child. Let me not be understood as here advocating a system of clothing too slight for the tender years of infancy, 1 am well aware ol the absolute necessity of warm clothing at that particular age. Rut all this may be secured without over-clothing. If we do not attend strictly to this view of the question, we create the very evils we are anxious to avoid, and in our blindness would point out a path for nature to walk in, fashioning into various deformities those helpless beings, in this state children are very irritable, and by their screams give sufficient indication of the painful leelings which this unnatural constraint of clothing creates. The evil is not limited to the simple control of motion ; the temper of the child, thus kept in a constant stale of inquietude, perverts all the secretions, so that the þÿhealth supply ot chyle is no longer furnished to the blood, for laying down new

matter for the growing child. Should the child be placed at nurse, its chance of permanent relief is then small indeed We cannot expect from nurses the same attention which mothers show. In nine cases out of ten, when children cry, it is from restraint, which prevents their playing. The nurse thinks she performs her part of the contract, if she supplies its food at regular hours, and secures it from broken legs and arms, by confinement. These, though good in their wav, are unfortunately often obtained at too high a price partial general bodily infirmity. þÿ Children, these good-natured nurses assure us, if left to themselves, are evermore getting into some kind of mischief or other, followed by deformities of the feet or legs. A threat of this kind, held out to a weak-minded mother, is sure to procure for the nurse a curie blanche to do as she pleases. It is scarcely necessary to refute the absurd notion of children becoming deformed by freedom of motion. Our West Indian settlements happily afford a satisfactory reply to such a statement, in the beautiful symmetry of the black and brown population, especially whilst children There the little negroes are allowed from the earliest moments to toss and tumble about as they may fancy, on the ground or matted floor, with no other covering than the sable one which nature has supplied. By this means every muscle being called into one kind of action or another, as long as the child is not fatigued, becomes beautifully developed,

and the fine athletic frames which they exhibit when grown to man's estate, has been ascribed by all naturalists chiefly to this cause. We can trace the effect of a good physical education still farther back, and to more classic regions than our sugar colonies. It is admitted by historians that the vigour and power of the ancients were mainly to be ascribed to the great attention which they bestowed on gymnastics. The clothing of children for all gymnastic exercises should be so loose as to offer no check to any motion or change of

position which in its sport it may choose j but, unfortunately, the taste which now pervades all ranks, in screwing up children in silks and brocades, holds out but slender prospects of this. Children are now paraded in our streets and public walks with all the affected gravity of age, and every natural impulse to riot or sport is instantly checked, because, forsooth, they are not graceful and dignfied ! The diet of a child must be of a good nutritious quality, to prepare healthy matter for its growing frame ; for. however well constituted the original disposition of organs may have been, they can at best but act feebly and imperfectly when the blood is impoverished, and deprived of those qualities so necessary, not only for keeping up the healthy action of organic life, but for laying down fresh materials for the growth and increase of the frame. The quantity and quality are two items in the diet of a child which demand the closest attention. In the early years of infancy, there is in the stomach and intestines of children an excess of mucous matter, which arises in almost every instance from overeating. To correct this, the first slep is to reduce the quantity of food, the next to ir/v prove the tone of the stomach by mild apeiients, regular open air exercise, with good but plain simple diet. If we do not succeed in removing this offending matter, there is, in a very short time, an almost perfect suspension of nervous influence, and the seeds of disease and deformity are thus laid down for the un-

happy child. These exhibit themselves undcr various forms. In some we see enlargement of the glands of the neck ; in others, swellings of the large joints ; in more, incurvation of the spine, enlargement of the head and beily, attended with great emaciation. þÿ In our attempts to fortify and strengthen the little sufferers, we must not resort to food of too stimulating a quality ; it should be plain solids, as roast meats, þÿW ith well-baked bread and light puddings; but all kinds of pastry must be scrupulously avoided For young children the limitation of meat is to be carefully proportioned the þÿchild growth, to s and the kind of exorcise which it generally takes There is, 1 think, an unjust prejudice against animal food for children. If fed exclusively on it, I am ready to admit its dangerous tendencies, as containing too large a quantity of highly-stimulating properties, which the infant years of a child cannot by exercise fair1 v distribute to the general system, but with proper limitations it is unquestionably the best. Vegetables, as being highly nutritious, should form a fair proportion in their diet, if boiled to a pulpy softness, or, as the French dress them, avoiding only the fatty matter which they introduce, they are highly nutritious; but unfortunately, the half boiled state in which they are served up, especially to children, renders them absolutely indigestible. þÿ It is hardly necessary to dwell on milk as an article of diet ; every one will admit its im-

portance. There are, however, particular seasons, at which I think it possesses certain properties more highly nutritious than at others. Of these the spring and summer I consider the seasons during which milk should constitute the chief drink of children At all seasons it is, it pure, a good article of diet tor children, but more especially in these two. I his is to bo ascribed to the qttanlitv of vegetable food supplied at those seasons, and which is so different from the dry, and in many cases coarse, oily substances winch,

From the St. Thomas Times , Wednesday September 12 1838. The Duke de Nemours has returned to Paris. The duke speaks in the highest possible terms of the Queen Victoria, of the British court, and of the reception he met with on the part ot the British aristocracy. Nothing can exceed his delight at the distinguished urbanity and deference with which he þÿW as treated in England ; and his surprise has not been less great than his pleasure at all the wonderful marvels of the British metropolis. As to Marshal Soult, who is still with you, he writes in the most glowing terms, and he declares that the 20 days he has passed in London have been the proudest and happiest of his life. One of his aides-decamp wrote to a friend of mine a letter, full of eulogies of the beauty of the British ladies, the admirable tenue of the British troops of the dignity and grandeur of the British aristocracy, and of the frankness, kindness, and heartfelt urbanity, of the British people. He states that Marshal Soult has said, þÿ Twenty such days are more than a reward for 20 years of actual þÿservice þÿ . St. James's Chronicle, July 14.

SPAIN. Madrid journals of the 18th and 19th inst., state that the government on the former day received dispatches from General Espartero, announcing his intention to quit the command of the army. If he were not furnished with a carte blanche to deal as he pleased with the forces under his command. He coin- I plained of being thwarted in his operations, and thereby incapacitated from rendering essential service to the cause of the Queen ! and declared to ministers that they must either acquiesce in his pretensions or accept his resignation The Cabinet held a meeting on receipt of this extraordinary dispatch, and after considering the danger of leaving without a chief the large force concentrated round Estelal. & the difficulty of providing a successor for Espartcro at a juncture so critical as the present, the ministers determined on declining to accept his resignation, and sent off a superior officer to demonstrate to him the deplorable consequences of a resolution which might compromise the fate of the army and country, and to pray him to continue in command of the army The answer of General Espartcro was expected with considerable anxiety.

Madrid journals and letters, dated the 21st inst. have been received. General Van Halcn had arrived in that capital from Logrono. j The resignation of Espartcro was still the | subject of general conversation, and the journey of his chief of the stall at such a moment was quite unaccountable. It is said that every one of the Cabinet ministers tendered their resignations to the Queen Regent on the morning of the 22d inst., but they were prevailed upon to remain in their offices.

The Vessel has therefore in all appearance been destined to sail along the coast or on Rivers ; it has been painted green under the Waterstreak, and has had a handsome Beak of variegated Festoons þÿ around the Windlass, whose fouifold Pall of cast Iron is marked "New Brunswick Foundry" was wound a chain of about 65 fathoms in length ; & foreward on the deck were found 2 Anchors with Iron Stocks. The Wreck must have drifted a long time in the Sea, as it was entirely covered over w ith Moss and impregnated with worms. From the Barbadian , September 1, 1838. Her Majesty's Packet Ranger arrived on Thursday evening, '27 days passage from Falmouth, and the mails were delivered from the Post Office the next morning. We give the following summary of the intelligence contained in the London Journals, from the 17th July to the 1st August : The Irish Municipal Corporation Bill has teen returned by the Lords to the House of Commons with some amendments þÿ The Church discipline Bill strongly advocated by the Archbishop of Canterbury, and as firmly opposed by the Bishop of Exeter, has been thrown out of the House of Lords, that is withdrawn for six months. The object of the Bill was excellent, that of more effectually p mishing immoral or profligate Clergymen, but the mode of doing it was objected to by the majority of the Peers, both lay and spiritual, as taking away too much of the power of the t> s lops, who already possessed too little for the due enforcement of discipline. þÿ The Irish Tithe Bill passed the House of Commons July 26th. in the Committee of Supply, one of the items was a vote of £500,000 to defray the expenses incurred by ti e insurrection in Canada ! ! ! In reply to a question by Lord Winchilsea, Lord Melbourne said, it was true that Sir John Colborne had asked leave to resign the command oi the Forces in Canada. W e find it mentioned in one of the papers, that Sir Edward Biakeney is to go out to Canada to take the command. Another baich of Baronets has been created by her gracious Majesty. One of the papers remarks, that Baronets are as plenty as "

biacaberries." There is no prospect whatever of a change of ministers, their position is firmer than ever- For the grounds of our opinion we rely on the statements of a very acute and impartial observer of political signs, the Editor of Bell's U eekly Messenger.

The Directors have now the satisfaction to lay before the Proprietors, in accordance with the provisions of the Charter, an account of the debts and assets of the Corporation on the 31st of December, 1837 ; and also of the profits made by the Bank up to the same period, viz. debts. dividend of two pounds per cent, be declared for the half-year ending 31st December, 1837, being at the rate of 4 per cent, per annum, on the paid up capital of the corporation, which will require 10,000 0 0

Leaving a reserve fund of £6,804 6 0 It may appear to the proprietors that the amount of profits would justify the directors in recommending a large dividend, but in the present early stage of the proceedings of the bank they consider it the better course to limit themselves to this amount. In their former report, the directors alluded to the difficulties they had to contend with, in consequence of the defective and unsound state of the currency in the West Indies ; and expressed a hope that ere long those difficulties would be removed by its settlement upon a sound and uniform basis. In this expectation they have thus far been disappointed, and they have consequently deemed it prudent to continue their instructions to their managers to proceed with the utmost caution in the issue of notes, and in the general conduct of their business This will account for the limited amount of their circulation, as shown by the foregoing statement. They have now the satisfaction, however, to report, that in consequence of their urgent representations, together with those of many deeply interested in the prosperity of the West Indian colonies, her Majesty's government have referred the subject to a committee of the Privy Council on coins, before whom such evidence has been laid of the defective state of the currency in the West Indian colonies as cannot fail to prove the absolute necessity of some remedy being applied. It has been recommended that the dollar, and its fractional parts, as the most convenient

and acceptable coin to the West Indian public, should be fixed as the general currency of the West Indian colonies ; and in the event of this recommendation being adopted by her Majesty's government, or of this question being settled upon any other sound basis, the directors look forward to increased facilities in the conduct, and enlarged profits as the result of their future operations As the committee is still sitting, the directors are unable at present to state the result of the inquiry, but they confidently hope that no great delay can now occur in some determination being taken by her Majesty's government on this important point. It affords them, however, much gratification to be enabled to say that the establishment is working well in the West Indies, and that even should they be disappointed in their hopes of an amelioration of the currency, they have abundant reason to anticipate that its profits will continue gradually to increase (Signed) John Irving, Chairman.

AFFAIRS ON THE EAST. The latest accounts from Constantinople are of the 4th and 5th inst. The Ottoman fleet sailed on the 28th ult., and was inet on the 1st inst. oft Gallipoli On the day previous to its departure, the Divan held a meeting, which lasted upwards ot 10 hours Nothing, however, had transpired respecting the result of its deliberations, but the French Ambassador, suspecting that the real object of the Captain Pasha was not, as alleged, to visit the islands of Mytelene Rhodes and Cyprus, but to land a force at Tunis, had dispatched orders to Admiral Gallois to keep a close watch upon the Turkish fleet The French Admiral had accordingly sailed from Smyrna for Vourla, in quest ofit, where he was on the 2d. with four ships of the line and seven frigates. It was reported, on the other hand, that Ahmed Pasha, on the fleet's arrival at Cyprus, would proceed in a steamer to Alexandria, and that he was clothed with full powers to effect a reconciliation between Mehemet Ali and the Sultan. l'he latter was said to have given bis consent to the raising of a loan, and authorised Ahmed Frozee Pasha to make arrangements to that effect with two London bankers. þÿ St. James's Chronicle, July 24.

The subject of the gold coinage is beginning to attrack the serious attention of the private bankers in the city, its depreciation in weight now causing an immense quantity of sovereigns to be rejected by the Bank of England, to the extent, some persons assert, of one-half of all the daily payments which are offered at that establishment. In this course the Bank of England, is justified undoubtedly, the object of the regulation being to prevent the practise of " sweating" the gold coinage, as that nefarions operation is termed, by which a number of sovereigns are shaken in a bag, which is afterwards burned, and the gold dust collected from the remains. Owing principally to this practice the depreciation in the weight of the gold coinage is so rapid that by experiments made at the Mint in the year 1333, it was lound that the sovereigns of 1817 had lost 8s. lOd in each hundred pounds ; those of 1821, 9s. 14 per hundred, those of 1825, 6s. 8d., and those of 1829, 6s. 2d per hundred; whilst upon the half sovereigns coined in 1817, the loss, according to the same experiments, was as great as 16s. 3d. per two hundred; of 1821, 13s. lOd. ; of 1825. 13s. fljd. ; and of those of 1829, 6s. 2d. per two hundred half sovereigns. At this time the quantity of gold rejected by the Bank of England, and by the Customs, Excise, and

Stamp-office, is so seriously complained of by the mercantile interests, that some remedy for these inconveniences and losses must he found, it is thought, before a very long time. þÿ Morning Chronicle.

The Temps (Paris paper) gives us the following coronation anecdote from a friend in London : þÿ ' Some of the attaches to our embassy paid dear for the pleasure of witnessing the wonders of the coronation. On the morning of that day they rose at four, dressed themselves in haste, and hurried to the Abbey, where they weie at once imppenned. They had made no provision for refreshment, and were too modest to ask a share of the savoury sandwiches which the noble personages around them had the precaution to bring with them At 12 they began to feel an appetite( at two began to feel exceedingly hungry, and by three were absolutely ravenous. The ordinance of 11th Novb. 1776, 10th July >778, 13th April 1779, 16th March 1792, and the 1st October 1802, together with the governor þÿgeneral p s lacard of the 10th Nov. 1823, with the exception of the instalments for paying the capitation tax have laid down the manner in which payment of taxes on properties in the westindies are to be paid, and tin; following rules are to be observed : That Negroes wilfully not given up by their owners or by those persons in whose possession they are, will be sold for account of the king, and the informer, if any. The capitation tax to the royal treasury is G4sk. W. C. for each town negro and Ps. 1 32sk for each male negro in the country, and to the land treasury Ps. 1 for each town negro and Ps. 2 for each male negro in the country, to be paid thus: Capitation tax not amounting to Ps. 20 immediately on taking up the list, but if Ps. 20 aud above that sum, in the manner specified in the ordinance of the 1 1th November 17761 That negroes born or dead in the course of the year, are not taxable, but they are notwithstanding to be regularly specified in the lists delivered. þÿ All other negroes are taxable, including invalids.

In like manner the lists of the estates must be made out with a true specification of the number of acres in canes, or in any other cultivation or pasture, tlie number of acres not used and the number of acres entirely useless þÿ In consequence whereof, the royal governments publication o the 26th of September 1833 is to be attended to ; Furthermore the names of the present owners, (as directed for the towns; together wall the names of all the inhabitants without exception, are to be specified on the lists. For the convenience of the community, and in order to obtain as much regularity, as possible in the tax lists, schemes have hern made printed by the lioyal westindia government, which schemes will be delivered gratis for the town of Ciiristiansted and its Jurisdiction, at the burgher connoils Incassator office and in Frederiksted and its Jurisdiction at the police office of that town. It is a duty incumbent on every owner of a house to announce himself as such, in writing to the commission to prevent anyd oubt who is to pay the house tax ; and it is further directed, that owners of houses, that have been vacant or untenanted for six months or upwards, and in consequence thereof are entitled to get a proportional reduetton in their taxes, are for that purpose, to come forward with sufficient proof of their assertion in order to enable the commissioners to observe the

needful in the protocol ; in which respect the Commissioners refer to the royal Governments publication of 20th October, 1836 It is to be observed, that the commission W'iil receive no tax lists, except they arc made out according to the above mentioned schemes, and every column properly filled up. It is however understood, that such lists are not required from owners of houses, who have only to announce themselves as such to the commission, though not occupying theirhouses, j as in such cases it will he considered sufficient when tiiey announce themselves as such, together with the names of the persons w ho occupy the house, in writing to the commisstoners. Separate lists duly signed by the owner or occupier for each house or plantation, is to he delivered to the commission notwithstanding the concerned individual might own more than one house or plantation. All houses in both towns are to be numbered, and the name of the streets to be be placed on both sides of the cornerhouses, painted with white on black ground or vice versa, in a conspicuous manner, according to Governor General v. Clausens placard of the 4th January 1777. In case of non compliance with the above, the following fines arc to he paid and levied for: Ten Pieces of Eight for every list that is not rendered in due time, it be either in town or country, and proprietors, giving in lists which do not contain the explanations directed according to the beforementioned schemes w'iil be subjected to the same fine, as the lists

in such cases will be returned to them. Owners of houses in towns, who neglect announcing themselves as such in writing are liable to the same fine. 10 Ps. for every house number that is either wanted or illegible, and the same for every streets name having the same defect. For all unpaid capitation tax under Ps. 20 a levy will he made within 24 hours after the

time, when the lists ought to have been deb' vered to the commissioners. Furthermore all persons are requested to bring the exact amount of the capitation tax to be paid to each treasury, as the time will riot allow to make change. This information is conveyed in the following telegraphic despatch, received at nightfall on Wednesday at the hotel of Count Mole, the President of the Council : þÿ

þÿ Lucerne, Sept, 20, $ past 4 p. m. þÿ THF FRENCH AMBASSADOR IN SWITZER- LAND TO THE PRESIDENT OF THE COUNCIL OF MINISTERS. þÿ The President of the Diet has this moment sent me a note saying that Louis Bonaparte, on the 20th ot September, addressed the government of Thurgovia, requesting him to announce to the Directory that he was ready to take his departure as soon as that authority should have obtained front the ambassadors of foreign powers passports for his preceding to a place where he can find a secure asylum. Jn this letter he speaks of his acquired rights, avoiding, however, explanations þÿon (Interrupted by the night.) To this intelligence our correspondent adds, that the French Government not con- j to i tent with the voluntary withdrawal of the prince, was determined on exacting of the .Swiss Vorct a decree of banishment against j Napoleon Louis Bonaparte, and that, in consequence, the march of troops lor the Swiss The National Guards of France have peti- ! frontier, already commenced, would continue. Should the French government persist, as wc have reasou to believe it will, in insisting on a decree of banishment against the prince, that majority will probably with the 2d j become more considerable, and more determined, and more angry. Cork, July 2t>, 1S38. þÿ Great interest has been created in this city, these few days hack, by the intended reception of a voting lady of tank and fashion in the religious community ol the Sisters of Mercy ; and the more particularly as it had transpired that the fair novice was not only allied to son e of the highest families in the kingdom, hut had also, in the exercise of an independent judgment, preferred the proscribed and persecuted doctrines of the Church of Rome, to the more fashionable tenets of its more favoured rival- Curiosity had been on the stretch for many days until at length it appeared that the young lady who had thus presumed to act and to think for herself was none other than Miss Agnew, a cousin of the famed Sir Andrew, and no less celebrated as the authoress of þÿ Geraldine," one of the best controversial ! novels of the day. The fame of Geraldine which had raised her high in the estimation of the literary and religious world, and her near connexion to the gloomy puritanical baronet of Scotland, increased the interest of the scene; and few things have produced more excitement in our social circle than the voluntary sacrifice ol this young and highlv gifted female, and the dedication of her future life, to corporal as well as spiritual wmks of mercy. has described under the admirably drawn character of þÿ Catherine þÿGraham in the novel. 1 hey were both dressed in lull bridal costume, preparatory to taking the veil, and resigning the world for ever; and as they km it at the foot of the altar, I could not hut flunk of the inscrutable ways of Providence, which sent these two ladies from Protestant England, to an humble and secluded cloister of the kind, pledge their vows and devote their lives to charity, in abused and Catholic Ireland. Such is the extreme barrenness of the London journals in the article of news, that we have found scarcely arty thing worth extracting, nor can we present our readers with a summary of intelligence worthy of their attention. The most gratifying part of this intelligence is to be found in the reports of the good health of our gracious young Queen, enjoying her Sylvan retreat at Windsor; and in the favourable accounts from ail quarters of the kingdom, of the harvest, though inclement weather in the preceding month had excited fears of bad crops of corn &c. An immense meeting of Radicals was expected to take place in the Palace yard on Monday the 17th September, when Home, Roebocr, Grote, &c. would agitate on Universal suffrage, vote bv ballot, and all other sorts of reform, as they call it, but meaning revolution. Whilst England is stirred up on these subjects, O'Cowkll is agitating Ireland on the repeal of the Union ; and Lord Brougham promises to agitate Scotland, These people are alarmed at the Conservative strength which has certainly increased during the last session. We have a bit of News from Canada' which is not at all unexpected. We had taken it for granted that the high-spirited and impetuous nobleman who has been for a short time administering the general government of the British American Provinces, would, as soon as he heard of the procedings in the

British parliament, indignantly throw up the power vested in hiin by his Sovereign, a power which has been designated as that of a Dictator, but which it seems has been grievously curtailed through the influence of a revolutionary patriot, Lord Brougham, assisted too by Conservative Piers, and by the desertion of his Excellency's friend Lord Melbourne. The Canada indemnity Act, and the censure bestowed upon the AToble Earl in the House of Lords, for his late banishment of rebels to Bermuda, must have arrived in Canada. United States papers of the 2t>th September, with which a mercantile friend has obliged us, inform us that the noble Earl, bad positively resigned the Government, and would depart for England, early in the present month, in H. M. S, Malabar, leaving, as we presume, Sir John Colbouiine in the Government of Lower Canada.

Whilst writing our Editorial this day, most unexpectedly the first October mails, not due until the 3d of November, arrived by her Majesty s Packet Lord Melville, Lieutenant Webb, in 21 days from Falmouth. This is the second time that this Packet has made a passage ol three weeks. Our papers will not be received in time for us to mc any use of them to-day.

This morning witnessed the awful and distressing spectacle of a human being launched into a dread eternity for a crime, which, though not actually perpetrated, was, nevertheless, proved to have been a premeditated intention to murder. Kennelly (as bis name is said to have been, in Thursday's Globe) a Private of the (3tith Regiment), had been tried oy Court Martial, and convicted of attempting to shoot Captain Nugent of the same Regiment, while passing him (Kennelly being 011 sentry.) The extraordinary, and we might perhaps say with propriety, the providential alertness and promptness of the officer in seizing tlie man's musket as tic was about to present it at him, saved bis life. It was reported, as we stated in our last number, that Kennelly was to have suffered death on Thursday, but the execution of the dreadful sentence was delayed bv the General Commanding the Troops, until this morning ; doubtless from the humane motive of allowing the wretched man a longer period to receive the consolations of religion, and to make his peace with his offended Maker. þÿ T his man was a Roman Catholic, and for his comfort and consolation, the Columbia steam er was despatched by order of bis Excellency Sir .Same >itu Wiiittingii.iM to one of the neighbouring Islands for a clergyman of that persuasion. T he steamer returned in three days, with the Reverend Mr. Carbeky ; and since Thursday, this gentleman has been engaged with the unhappy culprit in preparing him for the dreadful hour which was to sepa-

rate him forever from all earthly tilings, and carry him into the presence of his eternal Judge. We are informed that the prisoner was extremely penitent, and expressed his great consolation that his murderous hand was so promptly arrested, and that he did not take the life of his officer, though fie declared lie fully intended it. We have not been able to learn if be confessed to having find any leeling of dislike or revenge against the Captain, which could have wrought upon his mind so as to impel him to the crime of murder. It is said that Captain Nugent, or some other officer of the Garrison, was fired at the night preceding the one 011 which Kennelly attempted the life of Captain N. ; and he is jwsed to have been the gentry who fired.

Sometimes she escaped by accident, sometimes by stratagem, and now and then she boldly battled it out and was victorious. She was stunned, but never subdued; if her strength failed tier in summer's heat she rose refreshed in winter's storms, and won back among the Snows what she had lost among the flowers. Her nobles were often venal nay, traitorous, and her princes rash and weak ; yet her heart was sound and undaunted, nor did she ever want a hero of her own in the hour of need to succour and redeem her.

The Mormon War Ended. þÿ The St. Louis papers of the 8th inst. slates thai lire Mormon War had ended, by the surrender of the leaders of the Mormons. On the 28th ultimo about three thousand men, commanded by Oen. Atchison, of Clay County, made their appearance before the town of Far West, the county seat of Caldwell county where the Mormons were entrenched. Upon their approach the Mormons hoisted a white flag, which was shot down by Capt Bogard, hut was immediately replaced. Gen. Atchison then sent in a message, with a view to learn their wishes and intentions, when six of the lenders avowed their willingness to surrender, in the expectation that lite Mormons should he unharmed. The surrender was accepted þÿ and the individuals put under guard. Their names are Joseph Smith, Sidney lli gdon, George H inkle, Lyman Wight, Parley P. Pratt, and Mr. Knight. The Mormons assembled at Fur West, comprised 700

-- athsl " þÿ men under arms. Of this number, a smart body of 150, retreated and pursued their way to the northern frontier. On the day after the older of Gov. B"ggS directing the expulsion or extermination of the Mormons, was received by Gen. Atchison, disgusted with such a command, he immediately resigned his office, and retired. þÿ Subsequent to this, it is reported that a number of the Mormons were set upon and murdered. From the accounts which are now received, it appears that the poor deluded Mentions are "more sinned against than sinning1' in the matter of this war, and that their great error was in settling down on some of the richest lands of the State, and that in the defence of their right to them, against the avarice of others, they were forced to take up arms.

The Mormons have been thoroughly subdued and their leaders delivered into the hands of the military authorities sent against them. We are heartily glad to Iqarn that it is so. It may be that these creatures have been provoked into some of their enormities by the aggressions of the people around them þÿ we are inclined to think that it may be so, but, however it may he with others, it is quite impossible for us to ftel more than very slight sympathy for tliem. if they had been worth much sympathy they would not have been Mormons. A good deal of censure has been passed upon Gov, Boggs, of Missouri, for what was considered very sanguinary orders to the military officer sent against them. We must know more of those orders before we blame the Governor. N. B. Since writing the above, we have looked into the St. Louis Republican, whose editor is by no means a friend of the Governor, and the Republican says the orders have been misrepresented. That they were proper, and no more than were called for on the occasion. We dare sav.

Dundas, of the 83d Regiment, states that after a smart tire upon the wind nulls, the brigands were summoned to surrender which they did Eighty-six prisoners were immediately secured, and sixteen others, who were wounded, were removed from the mill, as soon as conveyance could be found. A large supply of arms, 20 kegs of powder and three pieces of ordnance fell into our hands. Some of the brigands effected their escape from the buildings in the brushwood, during the darkness of the night. 1 directed the militia to scour the bank, and several prisoners were then secured. Among others, a Bole calling himself Gen. Van Sault, who it is understood was the principal leader. AJ| the buildings adjoining the mill were destroyed, but the latter 1 directed to be occupied by a company of militia, and propose that it should continue to be so, or entirely demolished. 1 am happy to say, this service was performed with i lie loss of one man only, of the 83d Regiment. JbAlTSX TST'ilTiiSX iJAiKTitri w» Thouwaldsen. þÿ This eminent sculptor, whose statue of Lord Byron lias recently engrossed a considerable share of public attention, has completed at Home a work which is said to be his chef d'aeuvre. It is a statue ol Nemesis, which he was commissioned to execute under circumstances of peculiar interest. A young gentleman of the Protestant religion, named Miliers, was married to the daughter of one of the most distinguished Catholic families of Milan. The union was solemnized at Trieste, in which city marriage between individuals of the two different faiths is permitted. Unhappily the nuptual festivities wore soon changed to mourning. The bride died on the wedding day within a few þÿ hours after the nuptial ring had been placed on her finger. This melancholy event plunged the two families into the deepest grief, but no one was more afflicted than M. Miliers, sen , the father of the bereaved bridegroom, lu the hope of averting the serious consequences which his inconsolable sorrow seemed to threaten, his medical attendants recommended him to travel. Ho accordingly undertook a tour, in the course of which he visited Home. There he was introduced to Thorwaldsen, whom lie commissioned to execute for him a statue of Nemesis, whose power he had in so marked a manner experienced. Thorwaldsen was inspired by the tragical event, and he undertook to execute for M Miliers a basrelief, with the assurance that it should be entirely the work of his own hand, and that be would noi, as is customary, consign the

minor parts to his pupils. This splendid statue is just completed, and Thorwaldscn's Nemesis is the exclusive subject of conversation in Koine- This celebrated artist, though by birth a Dane, lias resided so long in Home, that the Italians are inclined to claim him as their own. He is a line looking old man. His countenance is characterized by intelligence and dignity, and is so expressive that an observer at a distance may, without hearing, understand the purpose of his conversation from his looks He is tall in stature. His hair is almost white aud his dress is as plain and unostentations as his manners. He has five ateliers, in which numerous artists are constantly employed. In the diilerent apartments he spends several hours every day : the rest of his time is spent in his own private study. His house is situated on the Monte Cincio, arid during the last thirty years he has occupied only the first story. þÿ On Sunday he receives company, and .hough visited by all the beau inonde of Home, lie never appears in any other eostuine than his robe de chambre. He himself perforins the dutv cicerone, describing of in all the valuable objects of art, with which his apartments are literally crowded. In tiis private character Thorwaldsen is a most amiable man. On young artists tie bestowes peculiar attention, and he receives them with almost paternal regard. Thorwaldsen has executed duplicates of all his principal works, and has bequeathed these duplicates to the city of Copenhagen, the
place of bis nativity. His daughter, who is married to an Italian Colour;!, is the heiress to his fortune, which, but for his generous liberality of disposition, w ould have been iinmense.
Mo dei. or the Battle of Wat nut oo. Lieutenant Sibom. the Assistant Military Secretary of Ireland, has arrived in London wi'.li his already celebrated model of the bat-

. UM'AL-W ffttSS . -Ai'-tle of Waterloo, which lie is now occupied in fixing up in the great room of Egygtiau Hall. In a few days hence, when this arrangement shall have been completed, the public will be gratified with a view of tiiis extraordinary work. The model has been many years in preparation. The survey of the ground lias been made under the direction oi Government, every kind of authentic information has been collected þÿ the number and position of the whole field has been modelled in the most the troops have been correctly obtained þÿ and i masterly and correct manner. The combatants on either side are shown, not by mere lines denoting troops, but by separate figures, exhibiting the troops in their various positions, and actions, and clad in their different costumes. The model represents the field of Waterloo and the surrounding country, extending about two miles and a quarter in either direction. It is reduced Jo a surface of about four hundred and twenty square feet, and contains upwards of 190,000 figures. As a topographical model, it has the highest pretensions, and is by lar the most beautiful we have ever seen It is constructed upon a scale of nine feet to the mile. Every house, everv tree, and even the slightest undulations of the ground, together with the very crops then covering its surface, have been carefully attended to ; but the arrangement of the troops is truly wonderful. Monday the 28tli instant the anniversary of the birth of our venerable and well beloved King Frederik 0 th ( who on that day completed his 7 1 it year), was celebrated with every demonstration of joy by all classes of the community. The guns from Fort Christiansvarn announced the return of the happy event at sunrise, by the discharge of a Royal Salute. The Government Packet Sclt'r: Vigilant, Captain 1) ahl repeated the same at eight o'clock. Inconsequence of sickness prevalent among the garrison and in the country, and to avoid exposure to the climate by the new recruits, His Excellency the Governor was pleased to dispense with the usual parade. At one o'clock a Levee was held at the Government House, which was fully attended by the civil and miltiary authorities and by a numerous concourse of respectable inhabitants of the Ishind and strangers now visiting it. His Majesty's health was drank with enthu. siasm under Royal Salutes from Fort Christiansvwrn and from H: M: Brig St: Croix, Capt: Schneider In the evening His Excellency Governor Souotker gave a grand Ball and Supper at the Government House to the Ladies and Gentlemen of the Island and to the strangers now among us. Their Majesties healths were drank accompanied with hearty cheers from the. numerous Guests, an I the company se perilled at a late hour, highly gratified with the urbanity and hospitality displayed by His Excellency, and animated with sincere good wishes for a lengthened continuance of health

and happiness to our gracious and venerable Monarch. By the Brig James, arrived at this port yesterday ft orn G uadaloupe. ; we. are happy to learn that that Island had not suffered materially by the dreadful earthquake of the lll/i inst:, although three distinct shocks were sensibly felt there þÿ The Captain reports that from 1500 to 2,000 lives were lost at Martinique. by that awful occurrence, and that Port li'ii/al was a heap of ruins þÿ we hear nothing yet from St: Vincents, Grenada, or the other neighboring Islands. «

From the New York Express, January 5 S ALE OF MORUS MULT1CAULIS. Some thousands of trees of this much sought for species of Mulberry were knocked off at auction on Saturday at increasing prices, and at no time has there been as many purchasers in attendance. The trees were from 2 to 3 and 4 feet in height, and brought from 53 cents for the smallest, up to 80 odd cents for the largest. Advices from Cairo of the 1st ult., published by the Augsburg Gazette of the 1st inst: state that " the English were daily extending their sway along the coast of Arabia and the Red Sea, and the garrison of Aden had been raised to 2000 men and placed under the command of a colonel. They had besides taken possession of the bay of Hovvakil, and of Harena, on the Abyssinian coast, and that it was through the latter point they intended hereafter carrying on the trade with Abyssinia, which formerly passed through Massana."

The Courrier Francais says, " We are unacquainted with the cause which keeps the archbishop estranged from the Court, but it is certain that he will not preside at the christening of Count de Paris, the celebration of which is positively fixed for the 1st ot May."

The Correo Nacional of the 1st instant states that a very warm explanation had taken place between Count Mole and the (Spanish Ambassador in Paris, respecting the meaning and accomplishment of the treaty of quadruple alliance.

A letter from Odessa, dated the 14th lilt., states that the entire of the persons attached to the Russian government of Little Russia during the administration of Count Woronzow had been culled together by the present Governor General (General Federoti,) by whom, in the name of the Emperor, they were all dismissed. Twenty-three of them were subsequently arrested and thrown into prison' The motive for this proceeding (surmised by the writer of the letter in question) was a suspicion that those persons sympathised iu tiie liberal sentiments of their late superior. A letter from Constantinople of recent date

" We are positively assured that the advances towards a reconciliation between Russia and England have been attended with complete success. About 150 English ships, hesides those of other nations, were daily expected there at the date of the last advices, the 23d of November. The Gazette de Smyrna, of Nov. 17, contains the following : þÿ The ancient town of Aden, capital of the small kingdom of which it bears the name, in the Yemen, is placed by the geographers in the Gulf of Aden, outside the Red Sea. The new town of Aden, by which name the English have just christened it, is at the mouth of the Red Sea, in the Straits of Babelmandei, a bay sufficiently spacious to contain a fleet and an infinite number of merchantmen of all sizes and which oilers always safe asvluni against the storms so frequent in these latitudes. This bay is open to the N W., and comes up to the town To the south of the bay, at a very little distance, and towards the middle of the strait, is the small island of Perim, the true gate of the Arabian Gulf, which the English fortified in 1799, and which they appear to wish to make a second Gibraltar. They are actively working at the fortifications of it; as well as on those of Aden, and when they shall be finished, the English will be able to monopolise the commerce of this sea. Even already a great many vessels of that nation make a considerable traffic by it of arms and ammunition, on the coast of Abyssinia as well as on those of Arabia Felix, it is in the direction of Mocha especially that their operations have attained to a considerable extension þÿ All the Mocha coffee which formerly went to quoted by the Augsburgh Gazette, says þÿ Egypt is, at present, exported by them to England. that the English have taken possession of Aden, the acquisition of which cost them but the moderate sum of 30,000 talari. It was a scheik or chief of a tribe whose name is not known who sold it to them lor that sum, and who after having given it up to them, retired with Lis followers into the interior of Arabia ; for one ol the principal clauses in the bargain was the retirement of the scheik to a certain distance from Aden. The East India Company, which has always seconded the government in all its enterprises, has not been found wanting in this circumstance, when their interests are most at stake. They have aheady expended considerable sums iu the construction of the projected railroads between Suez and Cairo, and iu the establishment of two inns which are nearly finished, one at Suez, the other about half way to Cairo While waiting the commencement of the railroad, they talk of repairing the road and of establishing between Suez and Cairo, lor the conveyance of passengers and merchandise, diligences, which will perform the journey in 24 houis, instead of lour days as hitherto. Already there is a regular service of steamers between Bombay, Calcutta, Ac, and Suez, and there is no doubt that these communications will become inoic active ami much more ficqucnt.

The Martinique Courtier of the 15th inst. furnishes the heart-rending details of the dreadful devastation caused in that island by the earthquake of the 11th. The late hour at which this paper came into our possession precludes the possibility of our giving a translation of them in our present number. We copy them, however, in French The town of St. Pierre has suffered considerably ; and the Courrier states, it will require 4,700,- 000 francs to repair the damage incurred by the buildings. As to Fort Royal, in the words of the same journal, " It no longer exists ! þÿ all the public buildings are levelled to the ground ; not a house of measonwork is left standing, and those built of wood, supported bv walls, have been also crushed by the falling of the latter. þÿ As to deaths they are every day being discovered under the ruins and rubbish. On the 11th, 586 bodies were interred in the burial-ground of the town only. The bodies were carried by cart loads. On the 12th, 273 dead were counted in tiie hospital and in the town, and on the 13th, this number was increased to 317 þÿ and that was not all !" The exertions of Governor De Moges, in honour of the dead, as well as in behalf of the afflicted survivors, have been most praiseworthy. The following proclamation was issued by His Excellency on the very day of the calamity : " Inhabitants of Fort Royal, " A terrible scourge has arrived to try " your constancy. Your houses are thrown " down ; you seek beneath the ruins, your " parents, your children, your friends. The

" King and France shall learn of so great a "disaster, and will come to your succour. In " the meantime, all those who let nothing dis- " courage them, who bear a human heart and " sound arms, will unite with the garrison and " the navy in exertions to afford a free course " to the water, to open the thoroughfare of " the streets, to prop up all that threatens "to fall, and thus prevent additional misfor- " tunes. The assistance of the King's Go- " vernment, and the help of the rest of the " colony less injured than your town, will not " be withheld from you, and you can assist " one another with your accustumed genero- " sity. " Inhabitants of St. Pierre, " 1 this instant learn that your city has also ' much suffered, as well as some divisions of " the island. I will make every effort to as " sist ond support you, and to repair the ills " that weigh upon you. " A De Mooes. " Rear Admiral, Governor." The ports of Martinique have been thrown open for the importation, by foreign vessels, free of Customs duties, of the lollowing necessaries : þÿ flour, beef, salt-fish, rice, corn, oats, lumber, and hardware ; and the exportation of bricks, tiles, and lime, has been prohibited. The Governor had also ordered that 12,000 francs be placed at the disposal of the Director ot the Interior, to be employed for the be; nefit of the town of Fort Royal. From the St: Thomas Times, Jan'y: 30. We have been kindly favored by a Gentleman with the loan of a newspaper entitled ' Diario de la llabana,' dated Jan'y. 1st, containing news from Mexico, to the 5th December ; and through the politeness of a friend who translated the accounts for us, we are enabled to give the particulars, which is as Jollows : þÿ na ," We extract from the " Diario de la llaba- 1st of this month, the following translation of an account relative to the taking and disarming of Vera Cruz. On the 4th December, the Admiral was apprized, by a letter from General Santa Ana, of the refusal of the Mexican government to sanction the capitulation of Vera Cruz ; the declaration of war issued against France and the decree of banishment of all Frenchmen from the Mexican territories. General Santa Ana and Arista were in Vera Cruz at the head of the troops stationed in that city, and were expecting further reinforcements : General Rincon- who had signed the stipulations entered into with the admiral, had been recalled to Mexico, and was on his way thither : the place having reassumed every appearance of hostility ; the admiral deemed it necessary to disarm it in order to render it incapable of attempting an attack. Accordingly on the 5th, before day-break, he landed part of the crew of the blockading squadron, and led them in three columns to the attack. The gate leading to the sea was seized upon, and the crew marched u; sword in hand, to the assault of forts Santiago and Concepcion, the former defended by 30, and

the latter by 15 pieces of artillery: ail the fortifications of the enemy, with the exception of one single bulwark, were immediately disarmed, their guns spiked and drived back from the walls, and the frames broken to pieces. After the entire victory which attended this expedition in which General Arista and many Mexican officers were taken prisoners, the Admiral ordered the re embarking of the troops, leaving the Mexican soldiers at liberty. General Santa Ana, while attempting to harass the troops by opposing their re embarkation, was most severely wounded, hav-

ing had his horse killed under him: the amputation of the leg became inevitable, and he is about undergoing a similar operation on an arm, little hope is therefore entertained of his surviving these tortures The Mexican troops under the command of General Ramon Hernandez evacuated the city and retired within one league on the left shore of the river of Vera Cruz. H. R. H. the prince of Joinville, who commanded, in this attack, the vanguard of the central column, greatly distinguished himself in the combat. The consequence of this battle has been the complete disarming of the fortifications, and the destruction of 82 pieces of cannon which have been put out of service. This victory has been achieved withoutthe least injury to the city, by special orders from the Admiral. The churches have been respected, even those in which the Mexicans had placed part of their artillery, as the Admiral preferred leaving those pieces untouch, ed which besides were few in number and altogether inoffensive, rather than contribution towards the least profanation It is highly honorable to all those who shared in this expedition to state, that during the four hours in which the town was in possession of the invading troops, not. a single door was lorced nor the least disorder committed. The loss on our side, as shewn in the following detail, has not been considerable. Dead Wounded Officers & Cadets 2 9 Sailors 4 37 Artillerymen 2 10 Total 8 56 Together 64

From the New l ork Weekly Whig, January 19, 1839. LATER FROM FRANCE. Paris, Dec. 15, The King of Holland, according to a letter from the Bas-Rhin to the Editor of the Augsburgh Gazette, has already appointed a Civil Governor for the Province ol Limburgh. The journey of the Emperor Nicholas to Moscow, accompanied by the Duke de Leuchtenherg, has been more rapid than had been imagined, his Majesty having set out on the 23d or 24th November, and returned on the 30th to St. Petersburgh. The Commerce publishes a letter of the 27th tilt., from St. Petersburgh, stating that the Emperor, previously to bis journey to Moscow wiili the Duke de Leuehtenbeig, has issued three ukusses. By the first, on account of the immense number of desertions taking place in the army employed against the Circassians, a pecuniary reward is granted to every subject of the Sultan who may arrest a Russian deserter, and gave him up to his officers ; the amount of the recompense to be determined by the commanding officer of the corps to whom the deserter may belong. The second ukase confers the rank of civil or military officer on the sons of civil and military functionaries of all classes, after they have served tiie state during four consecutive years. The third ukase ordains that the names of all the natural children of the lower classes shall be inscribed on the list ol the crown serf's, and that as such tliev may be employed hv the government in works ot colonization, or such others as they may be

ordered to execute. In a Toulon correspondence, quoted by the Commerce, we find an extract of a letter of the 21st ult. from Constantinople, which states positively that Russia had disgarrisoncd Abesia of the cordon of 16,000 men, who had previously covered the coast of that province, and who had been conveyed with the utmost expedition to Odessa, on board six ships of the line, and other smaller vessels, the number of which was daily increasing on the Black Sea, through tire unexampled activity which prevailed in the docks of Sehastopol. A letter of the 2lstultimo from Constantinopie states that the Queen Dowager of England was expected there, and that apartments were preparing for her Majesty's reception at the British embassy. Mr. Bulwer, who was on the point of leaving Constantinople, had been detained by a severe illness, which increased greatly after a long audience lie had of the Sultan.

The Royal Northern Antiquarian Society held its Quarterly meeting on the 6ih Instant: at this assembly, the direction in Token of deep acknowledgment for his distinguished merits, presented in the Name of the Society to the Sculptor Thorvaldsen (who for the first time as a Member partook in its proceedings) the lately published work A N TIQ UIT A TES A ME RICAN uE, or a Collection of accounts of the Voyages of Discovery to America of the antient Inhabitants of the North from the 10th to the 14th century, in which the Genealogical Register of Thorvaldsen , from Thorfinn Karlsefne, one of the most celebiated Colonist of America in the beginning of the Eleventh Century, is found. The Vice President Professor Finn Magnusen accompanied this with the following Address : þÿ In the Name of Our Ancestors! Welcome Noble Thorvaldsen to that Society through whose Labors they still live in the old Chronicles, these their Monuments, made imperishable bv the invention of Guttenbcrg. which you have so beautifully illustrated and designed. The greatest part of those men to whose exploits the Sagas bear testimony, were Inhabitants of the North, principally Danes. Norwegians, Swedes, Goths and Icelanders; and several also alike descended fmm the noblest families of England, Scotland, Ireland, Saxony and Frankony, and in some respects even from America itself, where one of your ancestors was born, about a thousand years after the beginning of our Christian -Era. I he Genealogical Tables by which

this is shewn, are contained in the present Work published by one of the members of this Society, and in which the very remark able though hitherto little known fact has been proved and established, that the first discovery of the New World belongs to our Northern ancestors. þÿ Your Name is one of the greatest Ornaments of this Work and therefore the Society presents it to Thorvaldsen himself, with the wish that it may meet his kind acceptance. It must be pleasing to you to see that the name Thorvald, which through you has been endeared to the world in general, and to us Inhabitants of the North in particular, was already borne in both Hcmisphers by your ancestors more than Eight Hundred years ago. It signifies one who has the strength of Thor, and fate had reserved for Thorvalds Son, thus to be sung by our immortal Poet þÿ Festivals of þÿSaturn. JJut it is not in Rome or for Rome alone that the Hammer of Thorvaldsen has been raised. His Sculptures out ot Italy's Marble Rocks now ornament the Churches and Palaces of our Capital, and Posterity will admire them in the Repository of those immortal works of which he has made a Donation to his Native City; also in distant Iceland, the home of thy ancestors poor in Gold, but rich in that Renown, which it has faithfully preserved ol its anticntlleroes and Raids. With this land we are closely connected, but the tie which unites us to it, is still further strengthened by your presence here. Denmark is the land of thy birth, and
the home of thy maternal ancestors; in you the Northern family arc united, as they arc in this our society, for the illustration and proþÿ I hor Ira Island i Rom vaukker Kronion til þÿLiv.

Thus is it a high festival to the Northern Antiquarian Society, to have you Noble Thorvaldsen, for this the first time among us, you wtio first taught the Proud Regions of the South, so richly gifted by nature, and embellished with those Noble Remains of Antient Art, to respect Uur North in the greatest artist of modern times, for in you classic antiquity lias again arisen, and moves from the banks of the Fiber to the shores of the Sound. True was the prediction of Thorborg, the heathen Vala, when she under the celestial girdle of the North Star, prophesied about the descendants of thy Mothers Ancestor, that they would be powerful, noble and glorious, and that more brilliant rays would shoot forth from them than her eyes could bear to look on. They are in thee concentrated, in that Sun of Ingenuity which illuminates our globe, which has inspired the cold marble with Divine Life, and which after its setting (which may the Almighty long delay) will shed an everlasting aurora over Denmark more brilliant even than tiiat which greeted you in ?resound and which announced your arrival to your Erethren of the North. DIED on the 5th inst, after a short illness, Mrs. Arabella Dill, with much truth it may be said that, that Lady was much respected on account of the many Christian graces which shone in her with undescmbled lustre. The word of God was the constant rule of her faith ; and to bring her actions to square with the same was her constant care She had a deep sense of human nature as fallen, and the necessity of an Advocate wiili the Father þÿ she was never ashamed of the Gross of Christ, and was alwavs ready to instruct the ignorant to virtue and to God, To enumerate the many virtues that ennobled the character of that Lady would be unnecessary, for they are too well known to the friends to need encomiums ; the gentleness of her manners, the affability of her address rendered her respected and beloved by ail who had the honor of her acquaintance. Consoling to her afflicted friends will long be the remembrance of those virtues, which blessed by the mercy of her Saviour, have followed her to eternal rest.

Prom the New York Commercial Advertiser, November 23, 1 838. BY THE PRESIDENT OP THE UNITED STATES OP AMERICA. A PROCLAMATION. Whereas there is too much reason to believe that citizens of the United States, in disregard of the solemn warning heretofore given to them bv the proclamation issued by the Executive of the General Government, and by some of the Governors of the States, have combined to disturb the peace of the dominions of a neighboring and friendly nation : And whereas, information has been j given to me, derived from official and other sources, that many citizens in different parts of the United States, arc associated, or asso- 1 dating, for the same purpose : And whereas, disturbances have actually broken out anew indifferent parts of the two Canadas; And whereas, a hostile invasion lias been made by citizens of the United Slates, in conjunction with Canadians and others, who, after forcibly seizing upon the property of their peaceful neighbor for the purpose of effecting their unlawful designs, are now in arms against the authorities of Canada, in perfect disregard of their own obligations as American citizens, and ol the obligations of the Government of their country to foreign na- Eons :

Now, therefore, 1 have thougt it necessary and proper to issue this proclamation, calling upon every citizen of the United Stales neither to give countenance nor encouragement of any kind to those who have thus forfeited their claim to the protection of their country ; | upon those misguided or deluded persons who are engaged in them, to abandon projects dangerous to their own country, fatal to to those whom they profess a desire to relieve, impracticable of execution without foreign aid, which they ennnot rationally expect to obtain, and giving rise to imputations (however unfounded) upon the honor and good faith of their own Government ; upon every officer, civil and military, and upon every citizen þÿ by the veneration due by all freemen to the laws which they have assisted to enact for their own government þÿ by his regard for the honor and reputation of his country by þÿ his love ol order and respect for Overformynderie den lOde þÿDecb r that sacred code of laws by which national intercourse is regulated þÿ to use every effort in his power to arrest for trial and punishment every offender against the laws providing for the performance of our obligations to the other Powers of the world. And 1 hereby warn all those who have engaged in these criminal enterprises, if persisted in, that, whatever may be the condition to which they may he reduced, they must not expect the interference of this Government, in any form, on their behalf : but will be left, reproached

by every virtuous fellow citizen, to be dealt with according to the policy and justice of that Government whose diminions they have, in defiance of the known wishes and efforts of their own Government, and without the shadow of justification or excuse, nefariously invaded. Given under my hand, at the city of Washington, the twenty lirst day of November, in the year of our Lord one thousand eight hundred and thirty-eight, and the sixtythird of the Independence of the United States. M. VAN BUREN. By the President : John Foksvth, Secretary of State.

Three peaceable lemale inhabitants of a country with which the United States are in profound peace, have been killed amidst their families and by their own firesides by a body of infamous scoundrels, raised and armed in the United States, and furnished with all the means of committing murder by sympathetic contributions from American citizens. And since it

at»3 has become known that the scoundrels have been completely cut off and captured or killed by the British forces, there is really a great outcry made about it, and the felons who have fallen by the men who were only defending their homes and their families, arc spoken of as being murdered ! LOWER CANADA. We have the Montreal papers of Wednesday, but they contain nothing of interest 'to our readers. We have also a letter from an esteemed correspondent in Montreal, from which we make the following extracts: þÿ I am happy to say that rebellion is entirely suppressed .in Lower Canada. The rising was much more extensive than that of last winter, but the principal leaders seem to have kept themselves carefully in the back ground, that in the event of failure they might be safe, whateve- should be the lot ol their followers. þÿ Sir John Colborne is of opinion that he has strength enough for any thing that may come against us in cither province. Two additional regiments, the 1 1th and 23rd, are on their way by water to Quebec from Halifax. The volunteers have turned out well. We can spare a few more regiments from this province for Upper Canada, if they should be needed. þÿ There are about GOO prisoners in our jaii, nearly all of whom were taken in arms. þÿ There is no doubt that many wiii be executed. þÿ You know the lion , a very respectable Canadian. I heard him sav yesterday that S'r John Colborne ought to hang ten or twelve leaders in each rebel parish. This, he said, is the only way to put down rebellion, and it it is not done we shall have a new one every winter. He said they ought to be hung in the parishes where they have been stirring up revolt, and their bodies be left suspended some weeks. This, he thought, is the only effectual way of suppressing re-

bellion. The habitans have no moral principle to work upon ; fear is the only thing that will have any effect upon them. þÿ 1 he prisoners in jail are living in great comfort. They are allowed candle-light all night, and many of them pass almost the whole night in playing cards."
